btos.label: Real estate and rental and leasing (NAICS 53)

name: Real Estate
blurb: Automated valuation is the sector's oldest AI and now federally regulated under FHFA and CFPB quality-control rules; plus valuation, leasing, and property-management platforms with methodology disclosed.

points.desc: Census BTOS reports real-estate sector AI use directly from firms.
points.name: Adoption is measured, not guessed

points.desc: The interagency Quality Control Standards for Automated Valuation Models - finalized by FHFA, CFPB, and the banking regulators - are the first binding federal rules for the sector's core AI: the models that value homes in mortgage decisions.
points.name: AVMs are now federally regulated AI

points.desc: The bureau's AVM rule page and its algorithmic-appraisal work are the record of how valuation bias and model accountability are supervised.
points.name: CFPB carries the consumer-protection side

points.desc: The National Association of Realtors' technology research tracks what AI tools agents and brokerages actually adopt.
points.name: NAR surveys the profession

points.name: CRETI tracks proptech capital

points.name: Zillow and Redfin publish their valuation models

points.name: Opendoor prices houses with models at risk

points.desc: JLL and CBRE - the commercial real estate services majors - deploy generative and predictive AI across brokerage, facilities, and portfolio analytics.
points.name: The CRE giants run enterprise AI

points.name: Leasing and property ops are automating

points.name: CREtech and MetaProp track the proptech market

points.desc: The Building Owners and Managers Association tracks AI in smart-building operations, energy efficiency, and predictive maintenance across commercial property.
points.name: BOMA covers commercial building operations

points.desc: The realtor association's technology accelerator is where residential proptech gets vetted and scaled - a window into which tools the profession is actually adopting.
points.name: NAR REACH backs the startups

points.desc: The residential brokerage's platform applies AI to agent workflows, client matching, and predictive listing recommendations.
points.name: Compass runs AI inside the brokerage workflow

points.desc: HouseCanary's valuation and forecasting models and Cherre's data integration layer are what institutional investors underwrite on - the wholesale side of the AVM story.
points.name: Institutional valuation runs on data platforms

points.desc: Prophia extracts terms, rent rolls, and obligations from commercial leases automatically - one of the clearest production uses of document AI in the sector.
points.name: Lease abstraction is a document-AI problem

points.desc: Visitt and Building Engines apply IoT sensing and machine learning to HVAC optimization, maintenance prediction, and tenant workflow in operating buildings.
points.name: Smart buildings close the operations loop

summary: Automated valuation is the sector's oldest deployed AI, and it is now formally regulated: federal quality-control standards for AVMs took effect in 2025. Valuation, leasing automation, 3D capture, and property operations are where AI actually runs; the regulator record and the platforms' own model documentation are the sources.

analysis.body:
Per the Census Bureau's Business Trends and Outlook Survey, 28.0% of firms in real estate and rental and leasing reported using AI in the most recent period, up from 25.6% in the prior period, making this one of the more measurably active sectors in the survey. The increase suggests continued diffusion rather than a plateau, though the figure still means a majority of firms in the sector have not yet crossed into regular use.

The most established AI application in real estate is automated valuation. Zillow publishes Zestimate home valuations for more than 110 million homes, using a neural network based model that draws on county and tax assessor records, direct MLS feeds, listing signals, and historical sales data, with the stated aim of reducing overall error rates while maintaining broad coverage. HouseCanary similarly offers AI-powered valuations, forecasts, and analytics across more than 136 million U.S. properties, applying machine learning and image recognition to assess property condition from photos. On the commercial side, Prophia uses AI to extract key lease terms from documents and combines that extraction with expert validation to produce structured lease data for portfolio owners and operators. Building Engines, a JLL company, positions its Prism platform as an AI-powered system for running commercial building operations end to end, with performance dashboards and actionable recommendations aimed at improving net operating income.

The consumer-facing and institutional sides of valuation AI now operate under binding federal rules. The CFPB, FHFA, OCC, Federal Reserve, FDIC, and NCUA jointly finalized quality control standards for automated valuation models used by mortgage originators and secondary market issuers in determining collateral worth on principal dwellings. Under that rule, institutions must adopt policies and control systems to ensure high confidence in AVM estimates, protect against data manipulation, avoid conflicts of interest, and conduct random sample testing. This is the sector's first binding federal AI regulation and it applies directly to the models that Zillow and HouseCanary, among others, produce or that lenders incorporate. Opendoor represents a sharper version of the same risk: its pricing models underwrite actual home purchases at balance-sheet scale, meaning model error translates directly into capital losses rather than simply a misdirected estimate.

On the operations and brokerage side, EliseAI deploys agentic conversational AI to handle leasing inquiries, schedule tours, follow up with prospects, and manage maintenance requests around the clock for residential property operators. Compass applies AI within its brokerage platform to agent workflows and client matching. Matterport digitizes physical buildings into 3D models and integrates with Procore and Autodesk, with stated benefits including reduced site visits and improved portfolio management. JLL states it has invested more in AI technology than any other real estate company, framing the investment as unlocking the potential of buildings and people across its brokerage, facilities, and portfolio analytics operations.

The organized profession and the startup ecosystem are both active. The National Association of Realtors tracks technology adoption across agents and brokerages, and its REACH program, created by Second Century Ventures, functions as a technology accelerator for residential proptech, offering a window into which tools are advancing toward broader adoption. The Center for Real Estate Technology and Innovation serves as a research and education organization monitoring the health of the proptech sector. CREtech frames its annual conference as the defining gathering for real estate in the age of AI, citing 3,000 leaders and more than 20,000 pre-scheduled meetings, which reflects the degree to which the commercial sector is actively coordinating around deployment rather than evaluation.

A decision-maker considering AI deployment in real estate faces a sector where the core technology, automated valuation, is now federally regulated and requires documented quality controls, bias protections, and audit trails before it can be used in mortgage decisions. Operations automation through platforms like EliseAI and Building Engines offers more immediate ROI pathways with lower regulatory overhead, though the sources do not report specific ROI figures. The gap between the 28.0% adoption rate the Census Bureau records and the level of activity visible in the commercial and institutional segments suggests that adoption is concentrated among larger and more sophisticated operators, and that smaller firms still have significant ground to cover before catching up.
